The authors focused on optimizing a single mixing element rather than the entire mixing section to reduce the computational complexity.
Free-form deformation (FFD) was used to parameterize the shape of the mixing element, allowing for a low-dimensional set of control points to define the shape.
The authors proposed a new objective function to assess distributive mixing based on the increase in interfacial area between the inlet and outlet of the mixing element.
The computational domain was based on a section of an unwound screw channel, with a height of 7.5 mm, a width of 31.5 mm, and a length of approximately 24.05 mm.

The material properties used in the study were: density (736 kg/m^3), specific heat capacity (2900 J/kg/K), thermal conductivity (0.4 W/m/K), and Carreau model parameters (A = 9.472 Pa·s, B = 0.1871 s, C = 0.655).

The authors used the steady, incompressible Navier-Stokes equations coupled with a steady heat equation to model the flow and temperature fields, and employed a Carreau model to capture the shear-thinning behavior of the polymer melt.

The Elastic Mesh Update Method (EMUM) was used to deform the computational domain based on the displacements of the boundary mesh, which was updated according to the free-form deformation of the mixing element's surface.

The authors divided the inlet of the computational domain into a grid of rectangular subdomains, tracked their deformation through the mixing element, and calculated the increase in the perimeter of the convex hulls as a measure of the increase in interfacial area.
The mixing element was rotated by 5.7 degrees in the negative z-direction to approximate the pitch angle of the screw in an actual extruder.
The authors used a velocity profile at the inlet with a maximum velocity of 0.027646 m/s, corresponding to a rotational speed of 8.8 min^-1 for a 60 mm screw diameter.
Slip boundary conditions were applied on the sides of the flow channel, no-slip on the bottom and mixing element, and a stress-free boundary condition at the outlet.
The temperature boundary conditions were 494 K at the bottom (screw) and 488 K at the top (barrel).
The authors used a reference temperature of 237 K for the Williams-Landel-Ferry temperature correction.
The length of the computational domain was chosen empirically to ensure no backward flow over the outlet boundary.
The authors argued that centrifugal and Coriolis forces are negligible and that the melt temperature is frame-invariant, justifying the use of the inverse kinematics approach.
